intro: `Git` is a free, open-source distributed version control system created by Linus Torvalds in 2005. It records every change made to a project so you can review history, undo mistakes and explore ideas in parallel.
Each developer keeps a full copy of the project history on their own machine, so most actions are fast and work even without an internet connection.

capabilities.title: Snapshots
capabilities.text: Every commit stores the state of your project, so you can return to any earlier point.

capabilities.title: Cheap branches
capabilities.text: Create a branch in a moment to try a feature without touching the main code.

capabilities.title: Local first
capabilities.text: History lives on your machine, so commits, diffs and logs need no server.

capabilities.title: Staging area
capabilities.text: Choose exactly which changes go into the next commit.

capabilities.title: Full history
capabilities.text: See who changed which line, when and why.

helps: Git lets you experiment without fear of breaking a working project. If a change goes wrong, you can step back to a safe state.
It also makes teamwork practical: people work on separate branches and bring their changes together through a shared remote such as GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket.
why: Older systems depended on one central server. Git removes that single point of failure because every clone is a complete backup.
Its branching model suits modern teams who work on short-lived feature branches, review each other's code and release often.

workflows.title: Feature branches
workflows.text: Build each feature on its own branch and merge it when it is ready.

workflows.title: Code review
workflows.text: Open a pull request so teammates can review changes before they land.

workflows.title: Releases
workflows.text: Tag a commit to mark a version you shipped.

workflows.title: Bug hunting
workflows.text: Run `git bisect` to find the exact commit that introduced a bug.

workflows.title: Open source
workflows.text: Fork a project, make your change and send it back as a pull request.

beyond.purpose: Rewrite history to keep a clean, linear log
Apply one commit from another branch
Check out several branches in separate folders
Run scripts automatically, for example before a commit
Keep build files and secrets out of the repository

tips: Commit early and often with clear messages.
Add a `.gitignore` at the start of every project.
Prefer small, focused branches over long-lived ones.
Try `git log --oneline --graph` to see branch history at a glance.
Practise resolving a merge conflict in a test repository first.
audience: Git is useful for developers, DevOps engineers, technical writers and anyone who manages files that change over time.
Whether you work alone on a side project or with hundreds of contributors, it gives you a reliable record of every change.
